title: Rockstar asks modders to please take its games very seriously
author: Lincoln Carpenter
content:
What happened

  • On September 10, Rockstar Games published new mod guidelines on its website, which it says are intended to "maintain a fun, creative, and welcoming place for players and content creators."
  • The guidelines are seem primarily targeted at mods for the FiveM and RedM platforms, which Rockstar acquired—along with their developers—in 2023.
  • Rockstar says mods must "respect our games": As part of its "right to set limits on how others can use our games and brand," the studio says mods can't expand or modify official storylines, missions, and characters, and can't combine settings and characters from different Rockstar franchises.
  • Rockstar says modders can't incorporate other intellectual property or real-world likenesses, and forbids cheat menus or modifications that interfere with its official multiplayer and online services.
  • Rockstar calls its official modding platforms "the exclusive licensed home for our community to monetize their mods," forbidding alternative monetization or commercialization of mods for its games.

Do these guidelines have any teeth?

Like Rockstar's more formal terms of service and platform license agreements, these guidelines are the sort of standard rhetorical armament a company equips itself with when in case it needs a quick fix for something egregious: If a mod emerges that could give the studio a legal or financial headache, all it'll need to do is tap the sign before giving the offending user-generated content the boot.

Of course, those guidelines are theoretically more difficult to enforce on platforms the studio doesn't own. For Rockstar, removing a mod that breaks its commandments is easy enough on FiveM. But if that mod's on a third party site—like the one our Josh Wolens used to murder a charmander on the streets of Los Santos—making that problem go away isn't so simple. House rules are a lot harder to enforce at someone else's house.

That hasn't stopped Rockstar in the past, however: In 2021, it sent takedown notices to a number of modding projects that reverse-engineered, restored, or reimplemented elements of older GTA games. It announced and released its trio of GTA Trilogy remasters later that year.

Lincoln has been writing about games for 12 years—unless you include the essays about procedural storytelling in Dwarf Fortress he convinced his college professors to accept. Leveraging the brainworms from a youth spent in World of Warcraft to write for sites like Waypoint, Polygon, and Fanbyte, Lincoln spent three years freelancing for PC Gamer before joining on as a full-time News Writer in 2024, bringing an expertise in Caves of Qud bird diplomacy, getting sons killed in Crusader Kings, and hitting dinosaurs with hammers in Monster Hunter.

title: Where Cities and Oceans Meet
author: Cheri Lucas Rowlands
content:
What does it mean to live in a disappearing place? For Pioneer Works’ Broadcast, Brad Bolman, a professor of history and environmental studies at Tulane University, writes about New Orleans, the shifting borders between land and sea, and the political and economic forces that continue to shape the city’s fate in a time of climate catastrophe.

If Los Angeles is the city that has been imaginatively destroyed again and again in film and TV, as Thom Andersen argues in Los Angeles Plays Itself, New Orleans is the one that has been destroyed countless times in reality. We have survived worse and rebuilt before, many insisted. We’re staying.

It was a reaction as understandable emotionally as it was disconnected from environmental reality. But that gap is a feature of life in the Crescent City. As I watched my first Mardi Gras parade this spring, junk falling in never-ending torrents from brightly decorated floats, a friend sympathetically interjected, “This must be driving you crazy.” What they meant was that as someone who teaches about environmental history but isn’t from here, I must be especially affected by the throwaway culture of the city’s most famous fête and its tons and tons of plastic beads, made from the same fossil fuels that are causing sea levels to rise around us.

title: Even Ed Sheeran’s Apology Took Both Sides
author: @NewYorker
content:
One of Ed Sheeran’s enduring contributions to the texture of twenty-first-century music—let’s say you are looking for one—will probably be the repopularization of the loop pedal. This is a technology, which Sheeran mastered in his early years as a busker, that lets a guy perform with himself, in echoes, alone, harmonizing with his own voice. The loop pedal allows the bedroom beat-maker and the YouTube singer to go out into the real world. It can turn an acoustic guitar into a threat. On his current world tour, Sheeran has spent a lot of time standing and looping alone. Ahead of his most recent performance, in Philadelphia, he had allowed one of his supporting acts, the rapper Macklemore, to be removed from the tour for saying the words “Free Palestine” onstage. Sheeran’s remaining supporting acts—the band Lukas Graham and the singer-songwriters Aaron Rowe and Finneas—and his backing band, the Irish folk troupe Beoga, all withdrew in solidarity.

The musical contributions of Macklemore have been fewer than Sheeran’s, yet morally clearer. At two previous concerts, in New Jersey, the Seattle-based rapper had performed his protest song “Hind’s Hall,” named after a building that protesters at Columbia had renamed for Hind Rajab, a five-year-old Palestinian girl who had been killed by Israeli soldiers. I had been orbiting the political side of Macklemore for some time—in 2017, he caused a similar news event by performing the anti-homophobia song “Same Love” at a high-profile sporting event in Australia during a gay-marriage vote, which I covered—and, over the years, I’d become warily appreciative of the rapper, best known, previously, for novelty songs and his earnest-white-boy persona.

In the lead-up to the concert in Philadelphia, social media had been flooded with mirror images of the same joke: “I’m trying to separate the art from the artist but the other way around,” of Macklemore; “I’m trying to think of a way to boycott Ed Sheeran’s music more than I usually do,” for Sheeran. It felt nice, for a while, to add to Sheeran and Macklemore two things that, respectively, they lack: politics and relevance.

Recently, the most exciting thing about Sheeran seemed to be his cowardice. A few hours before the show, a hundred or so local protesters gathered at a nearby train station. The demonstrators seemed embarrassed by the fact that they had been brought there by an Ed Sheeran concert. “Thank you for being here today for what I would like to be known as a show of support for Gaza and uplifting voices in Palestine, and not the ‘Ed Sheeran rally,’ ” an organizer in a blue shirt said into a megaphone. (A man named Mack told me that the focus should remain on Gaza, and he pointed out that tank shells used in the attack that killed Hind Rajab had been made by a Philadelphia-based weapons company, Day & Zimmermann.)

A protester named Asa Khalif, who wore a shirt that said “STOP GENOCIDE,” described Sheeran’s music as “beige and bland,” adding, “For those who are in love and want to have a wedding song—so be it.” He had a higher opinion of Macklemore: “ ‘Thrift Shop,’ I think, was genius. And it’s stood the test of time.” Another attendee told me, “I wouldn’t say I’m a fan of Macklemore, but I like what he does.”

How did the Sheeran fans feel? Outside the concert venue, a woman wearing a Taylor Swift shirt (she told me that she’s liked Sheeran ever since his appearance on Swift’s song “Everything Has Changed,” and “because he looks like Ron Weasley”) said that she was disappointed in Sheeran, but “sometimes singers can’t do anything.” (Reportedly, Sheeran had been asked to drop Macklemore by Robert Kraft, who owns the stadium in Boston that Sheeran is set to perform at next; Sheeran has said that the decision to remove Macklemore was made by the tour promoter.) The woman said that Sheeran had experienced his own troubles. “After his wife’s cancer battle, this might just be too much for him,” she said. “He’s, like, ‘Can’t we have one night of peace, every time I go do a concert, and not think about stuff?’ ”

“I’m in agreement with Macklemore,” Rachealle Davis, a Sheeran fan from Scotland, said. Of Sheeran, she added, “I think maybe he should have grown a set of balls.” Still, an Ed Sheeran concert is a form of “escapism,” she said. “It’s easy listening. We’ve listened to it most of our life.” Two mega-fans, Eva Stevens and Kizzy Holton, wearing Sheeran tour shirts, had driven up from Maryland. “I think Ed is apolitical, period,” Holton said, approvingly. “I think that he kind of sits in the middle of all the issues.”

It has, arguably, never been more pop to be political. More than two thousand miles away and three weeks earlier, Daisy Chain Fields Music Festival, hosted by Olivia Rodrigo, had politics as its purpose. Hayley Williams, the lead singer of Paramore, recently interpolated the lines “Fuck ICE” and “Free Palestine” into a song, during a live performance. Stevens said the middle was now the most dangerous place to be. “Those are the people who get picked on,” she said.

I brought up Rodrigo and suggested that Sheeran, in his attempts to stay neutral, now seemed to be the outlier. “But you know what?” Stevens said, “That takes heart.” Holton agreed. We were standing near the stadium; a beautiful sunset was coming down over the parking lot. Holton said, “It takes courage to stand alone in the gap.”

I was curious to see how a concert with no opener would open. Now that the event was Mackle-less, ticket prices had dropped dramatically, but the stadium was fairly full. (I found a scarcely believable survey, conducted by the British phone company O2, that ranked Sheeran as the third artist that respondents were most interested in seeing live, after the Beatles and Queen.) Around me, in the nosebleeds, were a mix of children in big friend groups and softly bopping couples. The pre-show screen displayed a graphic of a peaceful, undulating pink wave.

Sheeran emerged—alone, in jeans and a blue T-shirt—to a huge cheer, and began with an apology. Reading partly from a teleprompter, he said he’d been “making mistakes” over the past week—he did not mention the names of any of his former supporting acts—and added, “What is happening in Gaza is catastrophic and unjustifiable.”

“Everyone here can stand beside people they don’t agree with on everything, but they can all agree on singing these songs,” he said, then strummed his guitar into “Castle on the Hill,” a frenetic, bass-drum-heavy track about being homesick and fulfilling your dreams. Fireworks shot up from the stage. (Usually, Sheeran starts each show on the tour with a song called “You Need Me, I Don’t Need You.” Not this time.)

The stage for Sheeran’s tour has a glittering circular screen set into its center, twinkling like a ring light. It reminded me of the Portal, the short-lived art installation in New York that allowed people to wave at—or, in some instances, flash—people at a matching screen, in Dublin. For the two nights that Macklemore had performed on the tour, he had used the screen to display images of destruction in Gaza, as though it were a grim magic mirror. Sheeran often used it to show his feet as they hit the loop pedals.

I had been waiting to see what would happen when Sheeran arrived at the middle segment of his show, which he usually plays with the Irish band Beoga. Before “Galway Girl,” a Sheeran song for which Beoga’s violinist, Niamh Dunne, had written the main riff, Sheeran announced that he had replaced them. “When my friends dropped out of this show,” he explained, he had turned to Alicia Enstrom, a violinist from Kansas, and a crew of stand-ins, who, Sheeran told us, repeatedly, had learned Beoga’s parts in three days. (He did not mention Beoga by name.) As they played “Galway Girl,” the screen displayed an Irish knot and flashed the colors of the Irish flag, while green-and-red fireworks went off.

Sheeran repeatedly said that his shows brought people together, and it was charming to see groups of friends, mostly young, turning and singing to one another. (I also enjoyed “Thinking Out Loud.”) But, for all the talk of Sheeran as easy listening and harmonious, I found the listening not so easy. In between songs, he kept talking about how this had been the worst week of his life, in a tone of self-pity. “How am I going to get musicians to stand onstage with me,” he asked, “in a week where no one wants to stand onstage with me?” Sheeran said that he had removed a B-stage—one that extends into the audience—because he was “afraid of what might happen.” At one point, he sat cross-legged and said that he wondered whether he “even wanted to be an artist at all.”

But everyone else seemed happy to be there, and cheered each message of neutrality. There was a moment, during the scripted mea culpa, when the crowd roared after Sheeran said that he wanted his shows to be about “humanity, not politics,” cutting him off before he could say, “But this is a humanitarian issue.” It reminded me, slightly, of a tweet that I’d previously thought of as a heightened piece of satire: “Just got back from the centrist rally. Amazing turnout. Thousands of people holding hands and chanting ‘Better things aren’t possible.’ ”

Sheeran said, in as many words, that he was glad nobody there was mad at him. It felt a little enabling. “I’m feeling all of my friends and family abandon me,” he said. “But I look at the end of the week and I see fifty thousand people who haven’t abandoned me.” He added, “I love you.”

The sense of atonement faded as the night went on. Toward the end of the show, Sheeran told the crowd, “The one thing that I would like to apologize for is the first bit of the show where it wasn’t about music, and I had to talk”—the apology. In the past twenty-four hours, other artists, including Jack Antonoff and Imagine Dragons, had said “Free Palestine” or appeared with a Palestinian flag, onstage. But, if Sheeran’s music is feel-good, then two and a half hours of Ed Sheeran had certainly made the artist feel better. He went offstage and returned in a bright-pink jersey of his favorite soccer team, Ipswich Town, with the name of the tour, Loop, in place of the team sponsor. The stadium staff readied more fireworks. The first song of the encore was “You Need Me, I Don’t Need You.” ♦

title: PlayStation reportedly dumped Hideo Kojima spy action game Physint over exceeded budgets, missed deadlines, and Death Stranding sales
author: Mark Warren
content:
Their enthusiasm physlled out

Earlier this week, Hideo Kojima-helmed action espionage game Physint switched publishers from PlayStation to Xbox, a leap across the console divide which might make it more likely to get a PC port. At the time, Kojima claimed PlayStation had tried to can the game, while the console makers tried to paint the divorce as an amicable split. Now, a report's shed more light on why Sony decided to ditch Physint.

According to the Bloomberg report, the answer is basically every reason you might think a cash-obsessed behemoth still reeling from a bunch of missed live service shots over the past few years would have to get cold feet. Apparently, both Death Stranding and Death Stranding 2 having failed to generate as much revenue as PlayStation hoped played a major role, but that general fear that Kojima games might not be the sort of money printing machines Sony envisioned wasn't the be all and end all.

Kojima Productions had reportedly missed deadlines on Physint, with PlayStation having gotten stricter about production milestones following the likes of Concord's quick demise, and the game was set to be well over budget while still years away from coming out. Also an alleged bugbear was the fact a permanent PlayStation exclusive wasn't waiting at the finish line, contributing to Sony's unwillingness to further open their purse strings for Kojima and co.

All in all, the list of sticking points are exactly the sort of justifications you'd expect to hear from a company probably slightly perturbed that in getting out of a union they weren't happy with, they've ended up handing their most famous competitor an easy PR win. It's arguably an indicator just how far up shit creek the games industry is in 2026 that the chance to boast about having a Kojima game in your catalogue and/or stand next to the auteur at one or more of the year's many showcases no longer seems to offset some or all of the niggling number concerns in the minds of every exec.

When even larger-than-life household names with well-established game-making reputations that big companies love to use to embellish their own are being hot potatoed around, what chance do studios without that in their locker have?

title: Next major Halo game being developed by Activision, as Halo Studios all but closes as part of Microsoft's Xbox restructuring
author: Robert Purchese
content:
A "purpose-built" team separate to Call of Duty will handle it.

Halo Studios (formerly 343 Industries) won't develop the next mainline Halo game because it's being what sounds like drastically reduced in size. Microsoft has instead given development duty to Activision, which is making "a new purpose-built team" separate to Call of Duty to make it.

"We are eliminating 268 roles across Halo Studios, other first-party studios, and the XGS management and central functions layer," Xbox Studios boss Matt Booty wrote in a statement. "Activision will also be developing the next Halo title, led by a new, purpose-built team that is separate from ongoing development and plans for Call of Duty. A small team at Halo Studios will continue supporting the Halo community and games in-market," Booty wrote.

In a statement provided to Kotaku, Activision president Rob Kostich said: "We're thrilled to welcome Halo, Rare, and World's Edge to Activision." (Rare is also going to Activision.) "It's an honor and a responsibility that we do not take lightly. These teams and their games have inspired fans around the world for decades.

"For Halo, our goal is clear: make the greatest Halo game ever, worthy of its universe and legacy, while staying true to what made players love it in the first place. It is a bold ambition, one that this franchise deserves. We have already begun assembling a purpose-built team, unique in capability and talent, ready and excited to deliver this next chapter with the community."

The news arrives as part of another wave of major Microsoft Xbox restructuring, which has seen hundreds more people lose their jobs, British studio Ninja Theory close, and studios like Obsidian and Rare, as mentioned, consolidated into being controlled by others.

The Halo series, originated by Bungie, was overseen by 343 Industries/Halo Studios ever since Bungie bought its independence from Microsoft in 2007. Halo Studios (it rebranded in 2024) made a number of mainline Halo games, including 2012's Halo 4, 2015's Halo 5: Guardians, 2021's Halo Infinite, and most recently the reboot of Halo 1, Halo: Campaign Evolved.

Halo Studios also collaborated on every other Halo project, including 2014's Halo: The Master Chief Collection and the Halo Wars games. This move by Microsoft is, then, a significant departure for the Halo series.

title: 'The Hunt for Gisco's Treasure' walkthrough in Fire Emblem Fortune's Weave
author: @FionnTheBrave
content:
Follow

Link copied to clipboard

Published Sep 22, 2026, 4:27 PM EDT

Fame and fortune don't await you, but you get some nice stuff anyway

Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave's "The Hunt for Gisco's Treasure" quest is, at a glance, the ideal quest. You can stay in Dagsion to complete it, and you get a decent bit of money and renown when you do. Depending on where you travel in the city and how much you take in the sights, though, there's a chance you'll have no clue where to look for this little scavenger hunt.

Below, we show you how to clear "The Hunt for Gisco's Treasure" in Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave.

'The Hunt for Gisco's Treasure' walkthrough in Fire Emblem Fortune's Weave

The quest giver has a little scrap of a riddle to help guide you. "A colossus gazes upon Baal's waters. On the stone where she points, something worthy of note." Way back when you start someone's Act 1, Seteth's narration tells you the lake surrounding Dagsion is called Lake Baal, so that's the first clue. You're hunting for something overlooking the lake, which means the port in Lowtown is the best place to go.

Happily, there's just one statue in Lowtown, just east of the Vandahl Trading Company. She's pointing east-ish, but there's no item or treasure trove or anything in sight other than a wall. That's because the treasure is on the other side of the wall, along the little path that takes you down to the harbor side.

Grab it, head back to the quest giver, and you'll get your reward: a Morfis Almanac book, 5,000 gold, and 80 renown. The book is an uncommon one, so it's a very good gift for book lovers and decent for those who prefer uncommon and rare items, like Talimun and Catania.

If you're new to Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave, we can help you navigate the complex paths of causality. We have put together explainers on which character you should pick first, how to change heroes, and if you should play in casual or classic mode, so you can set up the campaign according to your preferences.

Fortune's Weave is a massive game, that's why we explain how long it will take for you to finish it. As you progress through the initial Heroic Games matches, you should focus on recruiting more characters, unlocking Boons of Salvation, and spending free time in the best way possible. Just don't forget to visit the Perch and have a quick Bird Time session.

title: It’s not just screen time: kids are bombarded by hectic media | Aeon Essays
content:
I am at the airport gate waiting to depart, watching passengers hurry past with rolling suitcases and paper cups of coffee. A small boy sits very still beside his mother. He holds an iPad close to his chest, almost in a cramp, clutching the screen as if it might otherwise run away. I hear loud clapping hands and squeaking children’s voices. I lean over and see a cartoon character in green snatch a toy from another character in pink. The pink character begins to cry, tears splashing from enormous eyes like sprinkles. The green character shouts sorry. Instantly, the tears stop and a wide smile replaces the tears before I have blinked. And, before I have even worked out whether the characters are speaking English or Arabic (as the mother does to the boy), the scene has changed and the two characters are rowing a boat with a random song in the background. The boy’s eyes dart on the screen from right to left, centre, down. His body is still but his attention is being hurried from cue to cue.

This is the problem I have come to think of as the pace of children’s media.

Children’s media are usually judged by their content and quantity: how many minutes watched and whether it was educational, age-appropriate, diverse, prosocial, commercial or safe. These questions matter and, with my colleagues, I have studied them through experiments and contributed to guidelines, regulations, or toolkits for designers. But we have been missing a bigger design feature that may be just as consequential: the time a medium gives a child to make meaning. A programme or app can contain good lessons and still move too quickly for those lessons to settle. For instance, in the US animated educational series Ask the StoryBots (2016-20), the subject matter may be genuinely rich – why the sky is blue, how eyes work, or where planets come from – but the explanation unfolds through rapid jokes, songs, visual shifts and sudden changes in style. Before a child has time to sit with one image or idea, the scene has moved on to the next, with a burst of information.

Different media have different temporal demands: a digital picture book, a game, a television episode and an app each ask a child to attend differently. But, across media, the important question is whether the pace suits the experience that the narrative claims to support. Does it give children time to follow a story, grasp a concept, identify with a character, regulate emotion or share attention with another person? Or does it continually hurry them toward the next cue, the next reward, the next burst of stimulation?

When media move too quickly, the layers of experience collapse into one another. A child may laugh at someone slipping on a banana peel but imitate only the visible silliness, missing the anticipation and reversal that make the joke work. A character may comfort a friend, but if the scene moves on too quickly, the child has little time to recognise the repair, or imagine doing the same in the kindergarten room. To develop empathy in the early years, a child must notice that another person feels something different. That small act of crossing over takes time.

In this sense, pace is not a minor stylistic feature of children’s media. It is one of the ways media imagine the child. Is the child a consumer to be retained, a nervous system to be stimulated, a vessel to be filled with educational content – or a person whose attention is still forming, and who therefore needs time to arrive?

People who worry about children and screens tend to worry about violent content, advertising, or whether a phonics app calling itself ‘educational’ truly supports phonics. These are reasonable worries and I share them. But spend five minutes watching what many young children watch, and you will see how fast, loud and bright everything on the screen has become. It does not matter whether the child is watching on a smartphone in the car or on a television at home. The screen has inherited the adult logic of media design.

That logic is, for the most part, the logic of the attention economy. It overwhelms and overshouts, making it easier for the screen to steer the viewer. The attention economy has introduced a host of small design features for shortening time. The Like button is faster than writing an appreciative comment. A progress bar tells us how many minutes remain in an article before we have decided whether to read to the end. Increasingly, AI appears beside long documents with an offer that sounds helpful but carries a philosophy: this text is long; would you like a quick summary?

The child is swept along by urgency rather than invited to dwell on responsibility or care for the other

There are, of course, features that work in the opposite direction. The delayed message and the pop-up that asks: ‘Are you sure you want to delete this?’ are two examples. Such features interrupt automatic action and return a fragment of judgment to the user. A nature documentary with linearity and the interpretive presence of an adult voice is a great model for children’s media; for example, in the TV show Prehistoric Planet (2022-25), David Attenborough’s voiceover and the camera’s zoom-ins encourage children to look closely and wonder about unfamiliar life. But these are exceptions within a larger system in which speed is treated as the default.

When learning is crowded with content that keeps jumping ahead – a crisis appears, a mission begins, a spaceship launches, a door opens – the child’s attention is restarted as each problem is introduced and immediately solved. Such media may gesture at teamwork or perseverance, but the speed of the format leaves little time for those lessons to sink in. In the animated TV series Paw Patrol (2013-), for instance, a rescue is clear and reassuring: someone is in trouble, pups assemble, each uses a skill, and order is restored. Yet the movement from problem to rescue to resolution is often so efficient that the child is swept along by urgency rather than invited to dwell on responsibility or care for the other. Similarly, in the app-based game Hot Wheels Unlimited, building tracks and racing cars may suggest creativity and problem-solving, but the dominant rhythm is acceleration: boost, race, crash, win, unlock, repeat.

Research has told us many useful things about children’s media. We know that some educational television (like Sesame Street) can support learning. We know that some apps are better designed than others. We know that interactive features in digital books can help when they serve the story, and distract when they do not. We know that characters and narratives shape children’s ideas about identity, gender and social life. Pace cuts across all of these questions as the condition under which content becomes experience.

Screen time can run fast or slow. This is partly why merely clocking ‘screen time’ is too crude a measure. Two children may each watch 20 minutes of media and have entirely different encounters with time. In one case, the child is moved through a coherent story with pauses, repetitions and recognisable emotional beats. In another, she is pulled through 10 clips, 30 characters, flashing colours, sudden songs and rewards that arrive before thought has had time to form. The clock records the same duration but the child does not live the same time.

And parents are rightly worried: a four-year-old does not come to media with adult reserves of self-regulation. She is still learning how to stay with a feeling, how to wait for a story to unfold, how to connect one event to another, how to notice that a character’s sadness matters before the joke wipes it away. If a programme moves too quickly, it may encourage a child to expect information to arrive in rapid, constantly shifting bursts, making slower, more sustained forms of attention harder to tolerate. Stopping this vicious cycle starts by asking what exactly makes children’s media fast or slow.

A child can look intensely engaged while being given very little time to think

Don’t get me wrong, I am not saying that slow is always good or better than fast media. Some lively children’s media can be excellent; some slow media can be dull, inert or badly made. The point is that good children’s media give a child time to complete an act of attention. Bad media keep interrupting that act before it can become a memory or play.

When my research group compared children’s shows, apps and digital stories, we saw that pace can become a set of design choices. A story can move in a way that helps a child anticipate what comes next, or it can jump so quickly between scenes that cause and effect become blurred. A screen can guide the eye toward one important object, or fill the frame with competing movement.

This is why the familiar adult language of ‘engagement’ is so poor for children. A child can look intensely engaged while being given very little time to think. In the Children’s Slow Media Project, we have therefore tried to make these differences visible. We evaluate children’s media by looking at how these media organise time. We ask whether the narrative is coherent enough to follow; whether the sensory field overwhelms meaning-making at specific age junctures; whether the design builds in stopping points, where the story can be digested before it goes on. Does a piece of media allow learning to develop through meaningful repetition? And does a story or piece create openings for a child and adult, or two children, to notice something together?

When in March 2026 the UK Department for Education advised parents of children aged under five to choose ‘slow-paced, age-appropriate’ content, without saying what slow-paced actually is, our group sought to make the term concrete.

What makes a show slow or fast for a given child? It depends. Children differ by age, temperament, language, sensory sensitivity and circumstance; thus, without testing their responses, it is impossible to provide a firm recommendation: a show that suits one four-year-old may overwhelm another. We therefore give ratings only to provide a map for adult judgment. The ratings are illustrations, inviting parents to check whether their child is being given enough time to complete an act of attention.

The shows scoring highest on the slow rubric are those that leave room around the characters’ actions and allow the child to recognise the actions. Often there is a face, a puppet, a song, a greeting, a familiar body on screen that treats attention as a relationship. Indeed, the power of programmes such as the US show Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood (1968-2001), the Norwegian series Fantorangen (2007-), and the British shows In the Night Garden… (2007-09) and Teletubbies (1997-2001) lies in their ability to build a rapport with the child and then repeat, almost as in a ritual. Here, small acts and greetings or songs provide a familiar frame, almost like a safety net, within which new concepts can be introduced. In the Australian animated series Bluey (2018-24), play often begins in an ordinary family situation and develops into imaginative games that involve parents, siblings and friends; the pace can be lively, but it tends to return the child to pretend play, negotiation and emotional understanding. In the animated TV series The Adventures of Paddington (2019-25) – a British-French co-production – gentle mishaps are usually held inside a world of curiosity, politeness, family and repair, so comedy becomes a route into perseverance or social understanding. Such programmes are slow because they leave openings through which the story can travel back into meaning and play.

The child’s attention is kept in motion by a manipulative rhythm that continuously restarts attention with the next tune, next bright image, next comic beat

Conversations between characters are another way in which higher-ranked shows convey new concepts with appropriate pace. When introduced with context, a new word or idea might not be immediately clear, but the child can notice and infer. Over time, the child arrives at understanding, and this slow, even arduous process helps the concept stick. For example, in one episode of Daniel Tiger’s Neighbourhood (2012-) – based on Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood – Daniel is nervous about trying the swing. The scene allows that feeling to be acknowledged, sung through, and gradually transformed into confidence, with support from Daniel’s friend Jodi and her grandmother. Similarly, in the Sesame Street-based game app Elmo Loves ABCs, a letter is traced, sounded, repeated, connected to words, and encountered through touch and play.

The lowest-scoring media are those in which the child’s attention is kept in motion by a manipulative rhythm that continuously restarts attention with the next tune, next bright image, next comic beat, next loop of familiarity or personalised nudge. Instead of allowing the child to settle into the story, such children’s shows repeatedly pull attention back; the same is true of many preschool game apps built around loops of reward and progression.

Evaluating children’s popular media taught me that pace is a revealing measure of quality but also a proxy for a deeper question about the child’s agency, their own sense of self.

The real distinction is whether a medium leaves room for the child’s own attention or continually redirects it. When every pause is filled, every uncertainty immediately resolved and every wandering thought pulled back by a brighter cue, waiting and reflection can begin to feel intolerable. The child learns to reach for the next stimulus before the previous one has had time to settle. To give space for a child’s attention to drift inward, to reflect, is therefore to leave room for the child’s inner life. Slow media changes the relation between screen and child by saying: you may arrive at your own pace.

Some critics may dismiss slow media as nostalgia: a longing for the children’s television of the previous generation, or a privilege available only to parents with time and large bookshelves and big houses with quiet rooms. But that is a notion we should refuse. The attention economy has trained us to treat a child’s pause as a problem, a wandering gaze as lost engagement, and an unfilled moment as wasted time. The opposite is true – slow time gives children the space to perceive, process, respond and make meaning – and it can be designed for in children’s media.

Like energy drinks, fast media promise more capacity than the child actually has: more attention is supposed to lead to better performance. Fast media feel like an extension of the child’s energy, but the bargain is unsustainable and unhealthy. What looks like support can become dependency, and what promises engagement and learning is actually compulsion.

Children need media that do not merely occupy them, instruct them or keep them quiet. They benefit and grow from stories and shows that preserve children’s capacity for inwardness and their relation to others. In fast media, the child’s attention is continually propped up by the next stimulus. Slow media insist on the opposite. In the end, the aim is not to withdraw children from the digital world, but to make that world more worthy of them.

title: He Was One of the World’s Most Wanted Men. So He Bought a West African Country.
author: Seyward Darby
content:
Just a few years ago, Jos Leijdekkers was a gangster in Antwerp, working for a major drug lord. Today he’s the most powerful man in Sierra Leone, which he’s single-handedly turned into a crucial port in the transatlantic cocaine trade. European authorities haven’t been able to track him down. Can a journalist? Alexander Clapp details Leijdekkers’s remarkable, violent rise to power, while looking for the man himself:

“These kinds of people, we are always seeing them in Africa. They come, they disappear. But the moment we learned who he was, it freaked me out,” a local car-dealer who was one of the first people to sell a motor to Leijdekkers, told me. “I left Sierra Leone after finding out. I became really scared. Not small scared.” Sophie van Leeuwen, a Dutch correspondent for RTL News, told me she “had the strong feeling I was being followed by the secret police” during the first days of a reporting trip she took to Sierra Leone in February 2025. She was arrested outside a villa where Leijdekkers was believed to reside, informed that she had intruded upon a “special security situation”, and questioned for 15 hours. Her camera and computer were searched and scrubbed. The Flemish owner of her hotel was interrogated over her alleged role in seeding a European spy network in Sierra Leone.

One evening in the hills above Freetown I attended a cocktail party where Western diplomats mingled with aid-workers. “Careful with that,” a European mission head told me when I mentioned why I had come to Africa, swivelling her blue eyes round the room. A Norwegian mining investor assured me that there would only be one way of knowing whether I was making progress in my investigation: “The government will arrange a car crash for you.”

“Before Ryan Wedding landed on the FBI’s Most Wanted list as a high-level associate of El Chapo, he was a bright-eyed kid from Thunder Bay. The inside story of how an Olympic snowboarding prodigy became one of the world’s most dangerous and powerful drug lords.”

‘I Don’t Know That I Would Even Call it Meth Anymore’

Sam Quinones | The Atlantic | October 18, 2021 | 7,655 words

“Soon, tons of P2P meth were moving north, without any letup, and the price of meth collapsed. But there was more to the story than higher volume. Ephedrine meth tended to damage people gradually, over years. With the switchover to P2P meth, that damage seemed to accelerate, especially damage to the brain.”

title: My Two Front Teeth
author: Brendan Fitzgerald
content:
A shattered grin, a wornout crown, a discolored incisor. How do our broken pieces define us? For The American Scholar, Joshua Bodwell offers a brief autobiography in dental work, examining the ways in which a broken tooth and a handful of interventions shaped his self-perception over decades. He also chews over (sorry) a select literary history of teeth, from Chaucer to Raymond Carver, and seems to ask virtually everyone in his life about their own smiles. His essay is an engaging study of imperfection, of a type many folks live with but might easily hide.

I left my chipped tooth untouched for a long time. It continued to discolor. I suppose I accepted it. Maybe it did make me look, as my friend suggested, tough. At the very least, it gave me an air of wildness. Or maybe it was because I was without dental insurance and acceptance was the easiest path. For long periods, I forgot about my tooth entirely. Until, of course, I met someone new who would ask, assuming it was recent, “What happened to your tooth!?” With that I went tight-lipped.

Then a surprising thing began to happen. As I got older, became a father, moved into a more demanding career, I found that I thought about my tooth less and less. At least, I think I did. I mean, I must have: There are photos of me with friends from this period, laughing without reserve, my half fake tooth on full display. A strange thing was happening to my unchipped front tooth, too: It began to seem more perfect than it actually was simply because it shared the stage with a chipped partner.

title: Appendix to Barriers and Safeguards: Access to Assisted Dying for the Socioeconomically Vulnerable Harvard Law Review
author: @HarvLRev
content:
A Comprehensive Descriptive Means

  • Volume 139
  • Issue 8
  • June 2026

Where jurisdictions have not yet clarified their stances as to particular safeguards, this Appendix characterizes their approaches as “Unclear.” If a jurisdiction imposes a waiting period but waives it in certain cases, this Appendix categorizes the jurisdiction as imposing the waiting period restriction. This is because exemptions are offered on a case-by-case basis,1 so default waiting periods are barriers to access in themselves because patients are unable to predict, at the time they choose to initiate the assisted dying process rather than to engage in self-help, whether they will be eligible. In the context of assisted dying, advance directives allow competent patients to issue written statements authorizing health care providers to provide or administer fatal medication at a later date, when they may have lost decisionmaking capacity.2
